Can AI accurately grade? Students navigate Nicholls’ Turnitin grading system

Daniel Roy, Staff Writer • November 10, 2026
Turnitin’s website. Photo by Sharaf Maksumov
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:33
Instaread

Nicholls political science major Jallisa Mack recalled when her professor called her in for a conference over potential artificial intelligence use.

Mack said that Turnitin, a plagiarism detection platform, flagged her essay as 80% AI generated. When she put it in other AI checkers, however, it was not coming back as AI generated.

Mack said that, upon appeal, the director of the English department noticed many errors and did not think that she had used AI–and neither did the teacher.

“She didn’t believe it was AI, frankly, but the system Turnitin marked it as AI,” Mack said. “So she went with the system instead of actually going with her mind.”

Upon reviewing her old writings, Mack said the teacher stated that her writings were all very similar in style. 

But she still had to retake the class at first.

As universities and the world continue to try and understand the full scope of AI, many argue that universities must find a better way to use AI when it comes to grading.

Students’ Feelings on Grading with AI

Ken Roux, a junior biology major, expressed that he feels like Turnitin is a good place to start, but a teacher should use their years of experience and judgement as the main source to grade students’ work.

“I feel like they should really be reading into it and be like, ‘Well this is something a student would say. This is something a robot would say,’” Roux said. “When they just strictly go off AI percentage, I feel like they don’t even bother to read it as much.” 

Kane Austin, a senior majoring in psychology, had the same experience as Mack with the same teacher. He said his paper came back as 100% AI, including dates, quotes and even his name at the top of the paper.

When he went to appeal, he showed his Google Docs version history to the dean, who said that was proof that he had not used AI. According to Austin, the teacher then said that she would fail him either way, as he had missed more than four classes during the semester.

“It’s like it became personal at that point, you know. Because on one hand she couldn’t fail me for the AI stuff, so she just decided [that], no matter what, she would find a way. It seemed real childish,” Austin said.

With several other complaints from students in that class, the teacher was removed according to Austin and Mack.

Is it Truly a Major Problem?

Nicholls students are not the only ones who complained about the Turnitin AI system. 

Rihanna George, a junior criminal justice major from the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, said that her professor was really strict on AI and automatically docked points for whatever percentage of the paper came back as AI.

In her specific instance, she said that her final in the class came up as 17% AI and the teacher immediately took 17% from her final grade, along with still grading the paper. She said the situation made her extremely upset, as the deductions could either make or break her grade.

“I knew that I put in the effort and time to get the work done myself, so it made me upset that I automatically lost points because of an AI checker getting it wrong,” George said.

She said that there is a difference between a student using AI to write an entire paper and possibly using it as a tool to help, and that professors should take time to analyze the papers themselves.

“You can tell the difference between someone who actually put forth effort and someone who cheated their whole way through,” George said.

Professor’s Thoughts

Professors are the ones tasked with navigating the AI grading system and its ever-changing policies. Assistant Professor of Mass Communications Lance Arnold said that Turnitin should be a starting point, not the final destination.

He also said it should be used as a way to teach students, not always just to punish them. If he suspects a student of AI use, he takes a deep dive into their paper, as well as previous papers, to compare before jumping to conclusions.

He said the thing that upsets teachers the most is when they put in the work to critique and students submitting AI-generated work.

“I spend a lot of time on this and I don’t want to teach AI how to write. I want to teach you how to write. That’s the whole point,” Arnold said.

The accuracy of Turnitin is inconsistent according to Arnold, but he thinks it is still useful when used as a tool rather than the ultimate decision-maker.

“Use Turnitin and read the report, run it through something else and find other ways to check it to see if it’s consistent,” Arnold said. “I don’t think you just throw Turnitin away, but you use it as one of the tools. Especially if you’re going to have some serious consequences.”

Andrew Simoncelli, an associate professor of mass communications, said that he had students in an independent study submit papers that used various AI platforms. He put the information into Turnitin and the AI percentages ranged from zero to 100.

“So I understand from a student standpoint that you can’t just rely on Turnitin,” Simoncelli said.

Simoncelli proposed that suspicious professors could assign in-class writing assignments and compare it with their out-of-class assignments to see if the styles are consistent. But professors cannot certainly say that a submission was AI-generated just because it is better than how the student normally writes. 

“Ultimately, we’re going to need a big policy here on campus,” Simoncelli said. “Because is it an instructor trying to prove that they used AI, or a student proving they didn’t? Who has that burden of proof?”

Looking For Possible Solutions

Students, teachers and faculty are still navigating the relatively new and constantly-evolving system of AI and its place in academics. Students like George and professors like Arnold feel it should be used as a tool. 

Professors like Simoncelli do not use it often, but understand its inconsistencies and students’ complaints; complaints that students like Roux, Mack and Austin have expressed firsthand.

Ultimately, a variety of factors should be used to determine if a student’s work is their own. Relying on just one source can lead to problems for teachers and students alike. Universities also have to look into creating specific policies so that students and staff understand the scope of AI.
